description: The REST to WebSocket bridge every scrape goes through, for both the standard and the realtime instance: which game sockets are up, what the relayed commands cost, and whether the process is growing

panels.description: Game sockets logged in and answering right now
panels.title: Sockets connected

panels.description: Sockets the bridge holds but which are not logged in. Every scrape against one of these answers "Server not connected"
panels.title: Sockets down

panels.description: Rate of commands relayed to a game socket across the selected bridges
panels.title: Commands per second

panels.description: Share of relayed commands the game never answered within the one-second window. The scraper reads these as return_code -1
panels.title: Timeout share

panels.description: Restarts the sockets started in the last hour. A handful is normal churn; a burst means the game dropped the fleet
panels.title: Reconnects (1 h)

panels.description: Logins the game turned down: bad credentials, a ban, or too many attempts. Any of these keeps a socket down until its backoff expires
panels.title: Logins refused (24 h)

panels.description: One row per game socket, worst first. "Last frame age" is the honest liveness signal: the bridge pings every minute, so a socket that has said nothing for several minutes is gone whatever its state says
panels.title: Socket status

panels.description: How many sockets each bridge holds logged in, against how many it holds at all. The two lines parting is the fleet falling over
panels.title: Connected sockets

panels.description: Restarts started, by bridge. The backoff grows to an hour after five consecutive failures, so a flat line at zero after a burst may mean the sockets are waiting, not healthy
panels.title: Reconnections per hour

panels.description: Transport errors the socket raised and close frames the game sent
panels.title: Socket errors and closes

panels.description: Traffic on the sockets themselves, read and written. A bridge with sockets up but no frames is answering nothing
panels.title: Frames per second

panels.description: Every game command the bridge relays, busiest first. The answer time is measured on the answers that arrived, so a command with a high timeout share can still look fast

targets.expr: sum by (command) (rate(empire_api_command_duration_seconds_total{bridge=~"$bridge", outcome="ok"}[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum by (command) (rate(empire_api_commands_total{bridge=~"$bridge", outcome="ok"}[$__rate_interval])), 0.000001)

panels.title: Commands

panels.description: ok is an answer from the game; timeout is the one-second window expiring; not_connected and not_found are the bridge refusing before it ever asked
panels.title: Commands per second by outcome

panels.description: Time the game took to answer a relayed command, averaged over the answers that arrived
panels.title: Average answer time

panels.description: Resident set and V8 heap per bridge. These processes hold fifty sockets open for weeks, so a heap that only ever climbs is the signal worth acting on, not the absolute figure
panels.title: Memory

panels.description: Slope of the heap over the last hour. A leak shows up here as a line that stays above zero across restarts of nothing
panels.title: Heap growth per hour

panels.description: Delay a 200 ms timer actually suffered. Anything above a few tens of milliseconds means the bridge is busy enough to start missing the one-second answer window
panels.title: Event loop lag

panels.description: How long each bridge process has been running. A reset here explains a fleet-wide reconnection
panels.title: Uptime

panels.description: Runtime each bridge is on
panels.title: Node version

panels.description: Sockets each bridge has in its map, connected or not. It should match the allowed list of its instances file
panels.title: Sockets held

list.description: standard is the instance the hourly fill uses, realtime the one the storm and dungeon workers use
